target: Agent 1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers to voting by giving people time and flexibility.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give most workers time off to vote, because private employers are not generally required to close or provide paid leave. Low-income retail and service workers may still be scheduled to work or lose wages if they vote, so the holiday would not reliably remove the scheduling barrier and could even worsen turnout disparities by helping people with flexible jobs more than constrained workers.

target: Agent 2’s objection that a holiday only helps federal employees and leaves private-sector workers without voting time.
objection: A national holiday can be enacted with job-protected voting leave for all workers as part of the same federal law, so it need not be limited to federal employees. The holiday itself would also change school, business, and transportation schedules in ways that create more practical voting time for private-sector workers, especially in retail and service jobs.

target: Agent 1’s reply that the holiday could be implemented with added job-protected leave and therefore would fix the scheduling problem.
objection: Adding employer time-off or other enforcement measures is a separate reform, not something produced automatically by declaring a holiday. So the holiday strategy by itself still does not reliably ensure voting time for private-sector workers, especially low-income ones.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a federal holiday does not reliably give private-sector workers time to vote.
objection: A national holiday changes the broader social calendar even for private-sector workers: schools close, many businesses reduce hours or shut down, and transportation and community routines shift. That practical calendar effect gives many workers, including those in retail and service jobs, more opportunity to vote without needing separate job-protected leave.

target: Agent 1’s overall case that Election Day should be a holiday because it will increase turnout and solve access problems.
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is a weak turnout reform and does not meaningfully outperform more direct voting-access measures such as state laws requiring time off to vote or automatic voter registration. Because the holiday is less effective than those alternatives, policy effort should go to the more targeted reforms instead.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that a holiday meaningfully reduces the day-to-day scheduling conflict for millions of voters.
objection: Many of the voters most constrained by work schedules—especially hourly retail, service, and essential workers—would still be required to work on Election Day even if it were a federal holiday, because private employers can remain open and control shifts. So the holiday’s calendar change does not reliably create voting time for the people most likely to be blocked by scheduling conflicts.

target: Agent 2’s claim that holiday timing is not enough to improve turnout and that voters still face the same barrier.
objection: Election Day as a holiday does improve turnout conditions because the main barrier is that the election falls during work and school hours, and a holiday shifts that baseline by closing schools and changing workplace and community schedules. That directly expands the window for voting on Election Day itself, so it can improve participation even without other reforms.

target: Agent 1’s claim that a holiday calendar change will reliably shift real-world schedules enough for constrained voters to have time to vote.
objection: The holiday’s calendar effects—such as school closures and altered business hours—do not guarantee time off for low-income private-sector workers, who may still be scheduled to work or lose wages if they vote. Therefore the holiday may help people who already have flexibility while leaving the most constrained workers effectively unchanged.

target: Agent 2’s claim that holiday timing does not meaningfully address the voting barrier.
objection: A holiday gives people more time and flexibility on the actual election day because schools are typically closed, many employers follow holiday hours or close, and public routines change. It also raises the civic salience of voting by framing Election Day as a celebration rather than an inconvenience, which can support turnout.
